articles.title: Japan flash PMI holds at 52.3 as services gain offsets factory slowdown before BoJ
articles.desc: The survey gives the BoJ a mixed but broadly workable backdrop: steady growth and persistent cost pressure support further policy normalisation, while weaker hiring and softer demand argue for a gradual pace. For the yen, the data are unlikely to shift expectations much on their own, coming alongsid
articles.content: The survey gives the BoJ a mixed but broadly workable backdrop: steady growth and persistent cost pressure support further policy normalisation, while weaker hiring and softer demand argue for a gradual pace. For the yen, the data are unlikely to shift expectations much on their own, coming alongside this morning’s above-forecast core-core CPI reading. In JGBs, the combination of solid activity and sticky input costs is consistent with the market keeping a December hike in play. For equities, the slowdown in manufacturing new orders and export business is a mild headwind for exporters. Raw material costs remain a key pressure point, and sustained high oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict are likely to keep input cost inflation elevated into year-end. --- Earlier: Japan core inflation tops BoJ’s 2% target for first time since December, yen firms --- Japan’s private sector kept growing in October, but slowing factory momentum, weaker hiring and rising costs suggest the expansion is becoming more fragile as the BoJ weighs its next move. Summary: The S&P Global flash Japan composite PMI output index was unchanged at 52.3 in October, the 19th straight month of expansion but the joint-slowest pace since May. Services activity rose to 52.0 from 51.3, while the manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 from 54.1 and manufacturing output dropped to 53.1 from 54.9, a seven-month low. New orders grew at the slowest pace in three months, led by the weakest rise in factory orders since March. New export business rose at the softest rate in four months. Job creation slowed to a 14-month low, with services payrolls falling for the first time since August 2025, even as backlogs grew at the fastest pace since June. Input cost inflation edged higher on raw material and labour costs, while output price inflation stayed sharp but slowed to a four-month low. Business confidence fell to its lowest in three months, with inflation a key concern. Japan’s private sector continued to expand in October, but growth remained subdued as a slowdown in manufacturing was offset by stronger services activity, according to flash survey data from S&P Global. Hiring slowed sharply and cost pressures increased, adding to the mixed picture facing the Bank of Japan ahead of next week’s policy meeting. The S&P Global flash Japan composite PMI output index was unchanged at 52.3, marking the 19th consecutive month of growth but matching the slowest pace since May. Services business activity improved to 52.0 from 51.3, while manufacturing lost momentum. The headline manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 from 54.1, and the factory output index dropped to 53.1 from 54.9, its weakest reading in seven months. Demand softened. New business rose at the slowest pace in three months, as goods producers reported the weakest growth in new orders since March. Services sales growth picked up but remained modest. Foreign demand was still positive, though new export orders grew at the slowest rate in four months. The labour market was a notable weak spot. Even though backlogs of work grew at the fastest pace since June, firms were cautious about adding staff, and job creation slowed to a 14-month low. Manufacturers increased their workforces moderately, but services companies cut payrolls for the first time since August 2025. Manufacturers also stepped up their purchasing, building inventories of inputs at the fastest rate in almost four years, while supplier delivery times lengthened substantially. Price pressures remained a central theme. Input cost inflation edged higher and was marked overall, with firms pointing to higher raw material and labour costs. Companies continued to raise selling prices sharply, though the rate of output price inflation slowed to a four-month low. Businesses still expect output to be higher in a year’s time, but confidence fell to its lowest in three months, with inflation a key concern. Usamah Bhatti, economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said overall growth was weaker than the average so far this year. He pointed to signs of a shift in momentum from manufacturing towards services as the year draws to a close. Bhatti described inflation as a key downside risk for the private sector and said it will be important to monitor domestic demand, given that the BoJ has raised its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995. The survey was released shortly after national inflation data showed core inflation back above the BoJ’s 2% target in September, with the measure excluding food and energy rising faster than expected. Taken together, the data show an economy still growing and facing persistent cost pressures, but with signs of strain in hiring and demand. Final October data are due on November 2 for manufacturing and November 5 for services and the composite index. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Segregation, Placarding, Insurance: Vetting Hazmat Freight Services
articles.desc: Hazmat freight doesn't forgive ignorance. A dry-van load delivered late is a service failure. A hazmat load loaded wrong is a federal violation waiting to become a headline.
articles.content: Segregation, Placarding, Insurance: Vetting Hazmat Freight Services | Sponsored Content | wvgazettemail.com You have permission to edit this article. This post was paid for by an advertiser. The Gazette-Mail newsroom was not involved in its creation. Hazmat freight doesn't forgive ignorance. A dry-van load delivered late is a service failure. A hazmat load loaded wrong is a federal violation waiting to become a headline. Shippers of hazardous materials place a great deal of trust in carriers. That trust should be earned, not assumed from a signed rate confirmation. Segregation: The Rule Most Carriers Get Wrong It's the backbone of compliant hazmat loading, and it uses four simple symbols that carry serious weight. An "X" means two materials cannot share a trailer under any circumstances. An "O" means they can ride together only if separated in a way that prevents dangerous commingling if something leaks. A blank space means no restriction from the table. An asterisk flags additional explosive compatibility rules. Plenty of carriers breeze past the "O" designation. They treat it like a suggestion rather than a requirement. That's a problem, because Class 3 flammables paired with Class 5.1 oxidizers fall under that designation. So do Class 4.3 materials and Class 8 corrosives. The regulation doesn't specify inches. It specifies an outcome-based separation that works when things go wrong. In , segregation rules decide which classes can share a trailer, and a carrier that can't explain its loading plan is a red flag. If a dispatcher stumbles over basic segregation questions, the shipper is gambling with liability that no contract can fully shield. Placards used in hazardous material transportation let firefighters know what they are dealing with. They let inspectors know whether a load is legal. They let other drivers know to keep their distance. Their physical characteristics are important: not less than 250 mm2 in size, while the inner border line should be 12.5 mm away from the edge. Class number should be indicated using digits that should not be less than 25 mm in size. In case of bulk cargo, UN number also needs to be indicated either on the placard or nearby orange plate using digits not shorter than 65 mm. Insurance: Where Assumptions Get Expensive The federal minimum for general freight is set at $750,000. However, when it comes to specific types of hazmat materials such as bulk explosives, Hazard Zone A gases, and Packing Group I toxic materials, the minimum amount increases to $5 million. Insurance is the part of carrier vetting that shippers most often take on trust, and it's becoming the riskiest assumption to make. As a , jury awards of $10 million or more are climbing fast, and they push premiums up even for fleets that have never been sued. When verdicts exceed policy limits, carriers' assets become targets. When those assets fall short, plaintiffs look upstream. Carriers that assumed they were protected discover they're holding the bag. Hazardous Material Transportation: Vetting That Actually Works Vetting is not all about having certifications. Find out from carriers how they segregate their mixed classes of hazards. Find out who puts placards on them and how their correctness is ensured. If carriers leave the task of putting placards to the drivers in the docks, they are bound to fail inspections. Review insurance documents for hazmat exclusions. Some policies carve out dangerous goods entirely, leaving shippers exposed without knowing it. Review training documentation. articles.content: Williamson, Inc. is driving the conversation with transportation issues at Policy Talks | Calendar | williamsonherald.com You have permission to edit this article. FRANKLIN – The Williamson, Inc. Chamber of Commerce & Office of Economic Development is driving the conversation with an important issue at the final Policy Talks program of 2026. Williamson, Inc.’s director of government and community relations has invited Will Reid, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Transportation, and Sen. Becky Massey (R-Knox County), chair of the Tennessee Senate’s Transportation & Safety Committee, as guests. Reid and Massey have confirmed they will be the featured speakers on Oct. 30. This free event provides chamber members, partners and Williamson County residents with the opportunity to meet the community’s business and government leaders. The October Policy Talks will take place Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, from 7:30 a.m. to 9 a.m. in the Community Room on the Columbia State Community College’s Williamson Campus. A networking opportunity and complimentary coffee will be available from 7:30 a.m. to 8 a.m., followed by the program from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. Williamson, Inc. has partnered with Dave’s RemarkABLE Coffee Cart, a student-centered initiative serving coffee at community events while providing students the opportunity to gain vocational skills. Policy Talks provides a unique opportunity to hear firsthand from speakers with programs focused on a variety of topics. Winter and spring events are held January through May and frequently include members of Williamson County’s delegation to the Tennessee General Assembly. Dave Crouch, of Aspen Grove Asset Management, will moderate the discussion. Sponsors of the initiative include AT&T, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, WAKM Radio and the Williamson Herald. While the program will be streamed live on WCTV, Williamson, Inc. encourages you to attend in person. In-person attendees will have the opportunity to network with legislators and fellow community leaders. Policy Talks is free and open to the public, reflecting Williamson, Inc.’s commitment to transparency, civic engagement and informed leadership. Whether you are a business owner, employee, nonprofit leader or engaged resident, this forum offers a valuable opportunity to stay informed and have your voice heard. articles.title: US defense agency backs autonomously-controlled nuclear reactors for space missions
articles.desc: The new contract aims to produce both nuclear-tested hardware and the engineering basis for autonomous, actively-controlled reactor operation.
articles.content: US startup to build autonomous nuclear reactor for lunar missions The United States has taken a major step to advance autonomous reactor operation for national security missions. For this, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has awarded Space Nuclear Power Corporation (SpaceNukes) an Other Transaction Agreement (OTA) under the Fast Capacitance (Fat Cat) program. The contract supports development and ground testing of advanced reactor control technologies that extend the demonstrated capability of American nuclear power. The award extends a continuous line of nuclear power development and builds directly on SpaceNukes’ successful nuclear power demonstration heritage. “This award recognizes the maturity and continuity of the team that , built, and tested KRUSTY in 2018,” said Patrick McClure, COO of SpaceNukes. In 2018, key members of the SpaceNukes team, while employed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA, performed the foundational Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology (KRUSTY) work — conducting the only full-power ground test of a new American space “We are proud to work alongside Dr. Dodson and Los Alamos National Laboratory to deliver the next demonstrated step in American nuclear power.” Under the current agreement, SpaceNukes and Los Alamos National Laboratory will design, build, and conduct a follow-on nuclear ground test of a Kilopower reactor incorporating active control rod operation—an advancement beyond the passively controlled architecture demonstrated in the 2018 KRUSTY test. The Fat Cat program seeks to advance autonomous reactor operation for national security missions, according to a Two rival fusion reactor designs unite to tackle the toughest barriers to fusion power Construction of world-first waste-to-energy plant completed, offers over 90 % CO2 recovery Westinghouse to build first nuclear fuel plant in 50 years to boost US reactor output US: 2.5 GW hybrid nuclear plant built from 1,500-ton reactor blocks slated for Texas site 2,000 MW underground nuclear reactors planned for former US munitions depot The phased program structure includes design, procurement, and integration gates leading to the ground demonstration, producing both nuclear-tested hardware and the engineering basis for autonomous, actively-controlled reactor operation. Integration work will be conducted at SpaceNukes’ workshop in Medina, Ohio, led by Chief Engineer Marc Gibson. The work positions American industry to provide reliable nuclear power across a broader range of mission profiles, including those requiring dynamic power management and rapid response under varying operational conditions, according to the press statement. “There is no substitute for demonstrated technology when American national security objectives are at stake,” said Andy Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “This award lets us advance the work begun in the KRUSTY program and bring another tested capability forward for the nation.” The technology could have important applications in space exploration, including providing electricity for future Moon bases, scientific instruments and long-duration space missions. power can also be useful in locations where sunlight is limited or where solar panels alone may not provide a sufficiently reliable supply of energy. Similar systems could potentially support remote facilities and certain defense applications that require dependable power. However, these are potential applications of the technology rather than confirmation that this specific reactor is ready for operational use. The project is significant because it aims to move beyond demonstrating a small nuclear reactor toward developing a more advanced system capable of actively controlling its own operation. The next steps involve developing the design, integrating the necessary components and conducting ground tests to evaluate the controller’s performance. articles.title: 590 times performance boost: Laser-powered quantum sensor hits 100% optical contrast
articles.desc: German scientists have unveiled a new quantum sensor that could detect brain signals and enable thought-controlled robotic exoskeletons.
articles.content: Diamond quantum sensor could power mind-controlled exoskeletons Scientists in Germany have just presented a new diamond-based quantum sensor that could let people with paralysis control robotic exoskeletons with nothing but the power of their minds. Developed by a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Solid State Physics IAF in Freiburg im Breisgau, the sensor uses a laser system to detect weak magnetic fields with high sensitivity. It achieved 100 percent optical contrast and improved the balance between sensitivity and measurement range by a factor of up to 590 compared with existing technologies. The effort was led by Jan Jeske, PhD, a researcher at Fraunhofer IAF. Jeske, who heads the Quantum Sensing Group at Fraunhofer at the research institute, was the the first to come up with a theoretical model for a magnetic-field-sensitive laser system using diamond with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers a decade ago. “I am very pleased that we have now experimentally demonstrated the magnetic-field-dependent shift in the lasing threshold,” Jeske explained. The sensor could have applications in brain-computer interfaces, medical testing, navigation, and resource exploration. have a limited measurement range. At the same time, those with a wider range are generally less sensitive. This is why the team created a technique called laser threshold magnetometry. , which are, in essence, tiny defects in diamond crystals that respond to magnetic fields. An NV center forms when a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom in a diamond, leaving a neighboring spot empty. GM tests 300,000 battery designs virtually, wins EV pack approval in just one month US firm ships 14,000-pound turbine core for supersonic jets and 42MW power plants 28 sodium-ion materials reveal paths to faster charging, longer battery life World-first touchscreen built into garment showcased, displays videos, responds to finger presses 50% lower quantum decoding latency: US firm pairs custom silicon with NVIDIA technology Conventional diamond quantum sensors measure fluorescent light that is emitted by these defects. The new technology instead places the diamond directly inside a laser cavity. The NV centers interact with the laser’s light field, causing changes in magnetic fields to affect the laser’s output. Under certain conditions, these changes can even turn off the laser and result in 100 percent optical contrast. For comparison, most NV-based magnetic sensors typically achieve just a few percent. The system can produce with a power of up to 50 milliwatts (mW). These are much stronger than those from conventional sensors. Calculations determined that the technology could spot extremely , with a sensitivity below 400 femtotesla (fT) per square root of hertz (Hz) for each of the three magnetic-field parts, under ideal photon shot-noise limits. According to the group, apart from improving magnetic-field measurements, the find could also help people living with paralysis. These signals could eventually be transmitted through a brain-computer interface to control robotic exoskeletons. Other possible uses include detecting weak magnetic signals from the heart and muscles, improving navigation, and spotting underground magnetic anomalies. Still, the technology is still under development and has yet to be tested. “Our approach could resolve a trade-off that has long limited the development and application of magnetic-field sensors,” Florian Schall, a PhD researcher at Fraunhofer IAF and the study’s first author, said in a . “It could pave the way for a new generation of mobile, highly sensitive magnetic-field sensors.” Get the latest in engineering, tech, space & science - delivered daily to your inbox.
